Laboratory colonies of the Greater bandicoot rat (Bandicota indica) maintained under controlled thermal conditions provide detailed life-history data for this large-bodied murid rodent. At a stable ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], newborn pups exhibit a mean wet weight at birth of 9.43 grams [Wwb = 9.43 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial murid neonates that rely heavily on maternal care during the first weeks of life. This neonatal mass is consistent with the general pattern among related Rattus species, though Bandicota indica pups tend to be slightly heavier at parturition. In captive breeding enclosures, females produce litters ranging from 8 to 14 pups per litter [N_R_i = 8 to 14 pups per litter], a relatively wide litter size that reflects the species' high reproductive potential under resource-rich conditions. When combined with the observed frequency of breeding events—approximately 12 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 12 litters per year]—this litter size translates into a substantial annual reproductive output for a rodent inhabiting tropical agricultural landscapes.

Gestation in Bandicota indica has been documented at 21 days [tg = 21 days] under the same thermal regime, a duration that aligns closely with values reported for the closely related black rat (Rattus rattus), upon which the original estimate was based at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively brief gestation period is characteristic of small-to-medium-sized murids and allows females to complete multiple breeding cycles within a single season. Following parturition, the altricial neonates remain entirely dependent on the mother for thermoregulation and nutrition. The onset of weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 25 days after birth [tx = approximately 25 days after birth] under these standard capt at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]ive conditions. At this stage, the pups begin consuming solid food while still occasionally suckling, and the progressive reduction in milk intake coincides with the development of their own thermoregulatory capacity. The weaning age represents a critical developmental milestone that influences subsequent growth trajectories and the timing of sexual maturation.

Sexual maturation in female Greater bandicoot rats occurs relatively slowly for a rodent of this body size, with puberty being attained at 160 days after birth [tp = 160 days after birth] when animals are maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This estimate is notably longer than the 60-day figure sometimes cited in popular references from Wiki sources, suggesting that captive conditions at this temperature produce a more conservative developmental schedule. The extended pre-pubertal period likely reflects the substantial somatic growth required before reproductive activation, as Bandicota indica achieves considerably larger adult body masses than most Rattus species. Following puberty, females enter a reproductive cycle characterized by a postpartum estrus, enabling them to mate shortly after parturition and maintain a rapid succession of litters during favorable seasons. The relatively late pubertal timing, however, imposes a constraint on the total number of reproductive events a female can complete within her lifespan, potentially limiting population growth rates in environments with high juvenile mortality.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Bandicota indica in captivity, under conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is approximately 525 days [am = approximately 525 days], a figure derived from combining a one-year adult survival phase with an additional 160 days of post-weaning development. This longevity estimate, equivalent to roughly 1.44 years, places the species within the typical range for medium-sized murid rodents, though it is somewhat shorter than the maximum lifespans reported for certain Rattus congeners that may survive two years or more under optimal captive care. The relatively compressed lifespan reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward rapid population turnover, consistent with the species' role as an opportunistic colonizer of disturbed agricultural habitats. Senescence in aging individuals becomes apparent through reduced locomotor activity, diminished reproductive output in older females, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections. These age-related declines underscore the importance of early reproductive investment in maximizing lifetime fitness.

Integrating the available reproductive and developmental parameters reveals the remarkable demographic potential of Bandicota indica when environmental conditions are favorable. Under the standard thermal conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the combination of a 21-day gestation (21 days) [tg = 21 days], weaning at 25 days after birth [tx = 25 days after birth], and puberty at 160 days after birth [tp = 160 days after birth] allows a female born early in the breeding season to produce her first litter at approximately 181 days of age. After this first litter, females can produce a new litter approximately every 21 to 25 days following postpartum estrus, potentially achieving as many as 12 litters per year [F_R_i = 12 litters per year]. For male neonates, wet weight at birth averages 10.54 grams [Wwb = 10.54 grams], slightly exceeding that of females and consistent with a pattern of modest sexual size dimorphism at parturition. The total lifespan of 525 days [am = 525 days] constrains the total number of potential litters a female can produce, though under optimal conditions with abundant resources, a single female may contribute twenty or more offspring to the next generation within her lifetime at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C].
